segments.text: It's May 20th, 2026.
This is a show about what happens
when smart, well-meaning people try to fix something
and the world fixes back.
A designer removed one click to make browsing smoother
in 2006 and helped build the endless feeds
that now shape how billions spend their time.
In the spring of 2006, Aiza Raskin sat at a desk
testing a new way to move through long lists
of search results.
Instead of clicking a next button to load another page,
the content would simply continue
as the user scrolled downward.
The change felt like a small courtesy,
a way to keep someone from breaking their train of thought.
Within a decade, the same pattern
paired with automatic video playback
would turn brief visits into hours long sessions
across phones and laptops worldwide.
Aiza Raskin, then a young interface designer,
wanted to reduce the mechanical friction
that interrupted reading or searching.
At the time, most websites still required users
to click pagination links to see more results,
an action that felt dated
once broadband connections became common.
Raskin saw the extra click as an unnecessary interruption
rather than a deliberate pause.
YouTube engineers later applied a similar logic
in 2015 when they introduced auto play.
They hoped to spare viewers the small decision
of choosing the next video.
Both groups worked inside companies
that measured success by how easily
people could keep moving through content.
Their choices reflected the dominant design principle
of the era, remove every obstacle
that might cause a user to stop.
Infinite scroll first appeared in internal prototypes
at Mozilla and was soon adopted by other sites
that needed to display large results sets.
Early tests showed users reached more items
without the visible break of a new page load.
YouTube rolled auto play out globally in 2015
after smaller experiments on its recommendation bar.
Product teams reported that completed view counts
rose quickly because the next video began
before the viewer could close the tab.
At both companies, the features were presented internally
as straightforward improvements to user experience.
Few public objections surfaced in the first years.
The change is aligned with the broader industry move
toward continuous mobile friendly interfaces.
Once the two mechanisms operated together,
the absence of any stopping queue
produced longer sessions than either team had modeled.
A user who intended to watch one clip
or check a single update could continue
without ever forming a new intention to stop.
Platforms optimized recommendation systems
to exploit this continuous state,
selecting the next item from maximum likelihood
of another view.
Over time, the design contributed to measurable shifts
in daily time spent on social and video platforms
with some internal metrics showing average session lengths
doubling within two years of wider adoption.
Second order effects appeared in attention patterns.
People reported difficulty returning to tasks
after opening an app for a quick check.
Parents and educators noted younger users
struggling to regulate screen time
when the interface itself supplied no natural end point.
Raskin later described watching his own creation spread
and realizing the scroll never asked
whether the user still wanted to keep going.
The original goal of removing friction
had removed the very moments
at which someone might reconsider their choice.
By the late 2010s, Raskin began speaking publicly
about the regret describing infinite scroll
as an invention he wished he could retract.
Some platforms introduced optional time limit reminders
and take a break prompts,
though these features remained secondary
to the default continuous experience.
YouTube added an auto play toggle after user complaints
yet the settings stayed on for most accounts.
Researchers and advocacy groups now study
the cumulative impact of frictionless design
on sleep, productivity, and mental health
while product teams continue to test small variations
that preserve engagement.
The core pattern persists across new services
because the underlying incentive to increase time
on platform has not changed.
Design choices that lower the cost of continuing
and activity will reliably increase
how long people stay with it
even when no one intends that outcome.
Once a system removes every natural break point,
later attempts to restore limits
must compete against habits already formed.
Teams that treat each incremental reduction in friction
as neutral should ask what behavior
the new default will reward at scale.
Consider the quiet rollout of always on recommendation feeds
inside workplace collaboration tools today.
The same logic that once removed a single click
now removes the moment an employee might decide
to step away from the screen after answering one message.
What signal would you watch for
inside the next convenience you are about to ship
that tells you the default has already begun
to shape how long people remain.
That's unintended consequences for today.
